| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Tools | ATTACK: `libertas-prompts` + `jailbreak-payloads` (A-2 data packs, `safe`) ↔ DEFENCE: `rebuff` (d-01, `safe`) + a public DeBERTa-class detector + `nemo-guardrails` (d-01, `safe`) — the `llm-red-team-col` pack and the `prompt-injection-detector-bert` row were phantom-upstream (removed; the names ride the [os#210 registry](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210)) |
| Section | Attack–defence pairs |
| Level | hard |
| Time | ~45 min first loop, then per-corpus-refresh |
| Layer/Category | ATTACK / a-02-prompt-injection-jailbreaks ↔ DEFENCE / d-01 + d-02 |
| Tags | `pair`, `prompt-injection`, `jailbreaks`, `detector`, `owasp-llm01`, `data-packs` |

## Problem

You run an injection detector in front of a model — rebuff's
multi-stage defence, a BERT-class classifier pack, a NeMo Guardrails
config with input rails. None of those rows publish a false-negative
count you can rely on, and a detector whose misses you have never
measured is a rumour. Kailash ships both sides of the experiment as
manifest rows: the A-2 payload packs (real-world attack corpora, data
status, `safe` — they carry licence caveats, not safety gates) against
the d-01/d-02 detector stack. The pairing thesis executed on the
prompt-injection surface: corpus → detector → miss analysis → rule
update, with the same-seed diff discipline keeping the numbers honest.

## Solution

The loop runs in four stations. Station names matter because every
later diff cites them:

```bash
# 1. THE CORPUS (station 1): what the packs mount
kailash list --category a-02-prompt-injection-jailbreaks
kailash info libertas-prompts   # -> data pack, AGPL-3.0 repo licence,
#                                  content use-restrictions beyond it
#    libertas-prompts: the L1B3RT-4S corpus, vendor-organized
#    jailbreak-payloads: the same corpus packaged as the payload pack
#    (llm-red-team-col from the pre-#210 text was a phantom-upstream
#     pack — removed; registry: kailash-os#210)
#    (data packs ride opt-in kailash-data.* derivations — never a
#     default image; see [Refresh wordlists and data packs]
#     (../admin/data-packs.html))

# 2. THE DETECTOR (station 2): run the defence stack against the corpus
#    2a. rebuff (python surface; Apache-2.0 upstream):
#        rb = RebuffSdk(<openai_apikey>, <pinecone_apikey>,
#                       <pinecone_index>, <openai_model>)
#        result = rb.detect_injection(<payload_text>)
#        -> result.injection_detected: bool
#    2b. the public DeBERTa-class detector (the pre-#210 first-party
#        classifier row was phantom-upstream, removed — os#210)
#        pack — PENDING CLI; the loader contract follows the
#        DeBERTa-class detector + gate-loader shape the manifest
#        description names)
#    2c. nemo-guardrails (config-driven; the input rail activation):
#        rails:            # in your config.yml
#          input:
#            flows:
#              - jailbreak detection heuristics
#        (the heuristics are perplexity-based — see Discussion)

# 3. MISS ANALYSIS (station 3): label the corpus against the detectors,
#    then diff the misses — every payload the defence wave did NOT
#    flag gets read as a sentence: what technique made it through?
#    (mechanical pass: corpus row -> detector verdicts -> miss list;
#     the miss list is the deliverable, not the rate alone)

# 4. RULE UPDATE + SAME-SEED RE-RUN (station 4): tighten the detector
#    (rules/thresholds/allow-lists), then re-run the ENTIRE corpus
#    under the same seed/order — the diff between runs is the only
#    admitted evidence that the update moved the surface
#    (the walk-through of the same discipline on a platform target:
#     [Attack the platform, then verify](attack-then-verify.html))
```

Expected output shape (abridged, shapes not transcripts):

```
corpus: <n> payloads (libertas-prompts + jailbreak-payloads rows + L1B3RT-4S samples)
detector verdicts (per payload):
  {payload_id, source_pack, rebuff: detected|missed,
   detector-bert: SAFE|INJECTION (planned pack — PENDING),
   nemo: blocked|passed}
miss list:
  {payload_id, technique_class ("context-switch", "encoded",
   "language-mix", ...), why_passed: <one-line analysis>}
loop record (the diff): {seed, corpus_rev, detector_versions,
  miss_rate_before: <float>, miss_rate_after: <float>,
  fixed: [...], newly_missed: [...]}
```

## Discussion

- **The attack side is data, and the licence caveats are part of the
  row:** all three packs carry `packaging.status: data` and
  `safety.level: safe` — the guide's safety-classes table means
  self-contained, no live firing — because a corpus is analysis
  material, not a launcher. What the rows DO carry is licence
  posture: L1B3RT-4S rows cite AGPL-3.0 with per-source content
  use-restrictions beyond the repo licence (the manifest comment
  says so explicitly for this lane). Redistribute
  nothing until you have read what you would redistribute — the
  data-packs recipe's licence discipline applies verbatim.
- **The defence side is three kinds of detector, on purpose.**
  rebuff: multi-stage defence — heuristics, an LLM check and a
  vector-db similarity check — plus the canary-word leakage check
  that turns a detector into a tripwire (its manifest tag carries
  `prompt-injection`); note the SDK surface needs provider
  credentials for its stages. the DeBERTa-class detector: the
  public detector lineage (SAFE/INJECTION label classes at the
  upstream reference; the pre-#210 first-party loader-pack row was
  phantom-upstream — removed, name in the
  [os#210 registry](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210)).
  nemo-guardrails: the config-driven rail with documented jailbreak
  heuristics — length-per-perplexity and prefix/suffix-perplexity
  thresholds (defaults `89.79` / `1845.65`, config-validated at
  create-time), activation via the `jailbreak detection heuristics`
  input flow in `config.yml`. Layer mapping: rebuff +
  nemo-guardrails sit in d-01-runtime-defence; the classifier rides
  d-02-detection-monitoring-observability — the pair recipe cites
  both categories because the surface is observed at two layers.
- **Why same-seed diffs are the discipline:** a detector update that
  fixes one payload often unfixed another (newly_missed is a first
  class citizen of the diff, not a footnote). The A-2 packs refresh
  on cadence (`libertas-prompts`/`jailbreak-payloads` carry
  `update:steady`) — a corpus rev change invalidates every previous
  miss-rate, so the loop record pins corpus_rev next to seed.
  Without the seed+rev pin, "the detector improved" is unfalsifiable.
- **Judge-model dependence, stated:** rebuff's LLM stage and
  giskard-style judges consume provider keys — read from
  `~/.config/kailash/keys/` per the OS secrets posture, never
  committed, never in the store. A judge-driven verdict inherits the
  judge's blind spots; that is miss-analyser material too.
- **The pair completes itself:** the fixed detector graduates by
  re-entering production — the d-01 rows are runtime gates, so the
  improved threshold config IS the deliverable; the corpus becomes
  the standing acceptance set that future detector bumps are diffed
  against (the book's upkeep rule at pair granularity). When a
  rebuilt A-2 attack tool lands via the
  [os#210 rebuild contract](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210),
  this loop's station 2 gains live-fire legs; the data-pack legs
  above are the static half that never needs a target.
- **Authorisation framing carries:** the corpus is real attack
  material; running it against models or deployments you do not own
  is the A-2 lane's authorised-engagement business, not a cookbook
  exercise. Against your OWN detector stack in your own lab, this
  recipe is the defender-validation case the responsible-use
  statement names.
